description.summary: Japanese demons or ogres from Buddhist and Shinto traditions. Large humanoid creatures with horns, fangs, wild hair, and red or blue skin, often wielding iron clubs (kanabō).
description.full: Oni are supernatural demons or ogres from Japanese folklore, Buddhist mythology, and Shinto traditions. Typically depicted as large, fearsome humanoids with horns, fangs, wild hair, and red or blue skin wearing tiger-skin loincloths, oni carry iron clubs called kanabō. They serve multiple roles in Japanese culture: punishing the wicked, guarding Buddhist hell realms, and embodying human vices like greed, anger, and pride. Humans can transform into oni through extreme wickedness or curses. Oni remain a living part of Japanese cultural tradition through festivals like Setsubun, masks, folklore, and modern media.

etymology.origin: The word 'oni' (鬼) derives from ancient Japanese, possibly from 'on' meaning to hide or conceal, reflecting their invisible spiritual nature.
etymology.meaning: Demon, ogre, troll, or evil spirit

features.description: One or more horns protruding from head, typically two
Traditional clothing made from tiger pelt
Sharp claws on hands and feet

physical.morphology: Large humanoid with demonic features. Muscular build, often depicted with grotesque or exaggerated facial features.

abilities.description: Capable of wielding massive iron clubs (kanabō)
Can take human form to deceive
Associated with storms, disease, and famine

cultural_presence.significance: Central to folklore, festivals, religious practice

Continuous cultural presence in festivals, media, art

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Associated with Setsubun (early February) bean-throwing festival

origins.cultural_roots: Oni derive from ancient Japanese animistic beliefs, later incorporated into Buddhism and Shinto. They represent the intersection of indigenous Japanese spirituality with imported Buddhist concepts of hell and demons.
origins.earliest_accounts: Pre-Heian period oral traditions and early Buddhist texts in Japan
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to Chinese demons, Korean dokkaebi, and broader Asian supernatural traditions.

famous_oni.name: Shuten-dōji
famous_oni.description: Most famous oni, leader of oni on Mount Ōe, defeated by legendary warrior Minamoto no Raikō

famous_oni.name: Ibaraki-dōji
famous_oni.description: Oni servant of Shuten-dōji, known for severed arm legend

history.modern_era: Oni remain central to Japanese culture through festivals, traditional theater (Noh, kabuki), masks, tattoo art, anime, manga, and video games. They represent both fearsome evil and protective guardians depending on context.

traditions: Oni masks in festivals and theater
Tales of transformation from human to oni
stories: Shuten-dōji and the oni of Mount Ōe
folklore.beliefs: Oni embody negative emotions and vices. Humans overcome with anger, greed, or jealousy can transform into oni. Bean-throwing drives them away.

setsubun.practice: Bean-throwing ceremony (mamemaki) to drive out oni and welcome good fortune
setsubun.chant: Oni wa soto! Fuku wa uchi!
